claims.text: Conventional W–Cu composites have relatively high thermal boundary resistance at unengineered W–Cu interfaces.
Conventional W–Cu composites show variable irradiation responses.
The proposed intervention is sputter-deposition of a nanoscale interfacial layer on tungsten before consolidation with copper.
The engineered layer will create a coherent bonding network between tungsten and copper.
The engineered layer will reduce electron and phonon scattering sites at the W–Cu interface.
A controlled interfacial layer will minimize defects and mismatches at the W–Cu boundary.
Minimizing interfacial defects and mismatches will lower W–Cu thermal boundary resistance.
The engineered interface will resist irradiation-induced damage.
The engineered interface will resist mechanical degradation.
The interfacial layer will increase the thermal conductivity of W–Cu relative to an otherwise comparable unmodified composite.
The interfacial layer will not reduce mechanical strength relative to the unmodified control.
The interfacial layer will not reduce irradiation stability relative to the unmodified control.
The predicted benefits will persist under high heat flux and moderate-to-high irradiation characteristic of fusion-reactor joints.
Prior trends in interface engineering are promising for simultaneous thermal and mechanical improvement.
The long-term irradiation resistance of the engineered layer remains empirically unvalidated.
